### B.1 Proof of Lemma 3.5

See 3.5

#### Proof.

The graph $G$ is constructed as follows. For simplicity, we first consider the directed setting by constructing DAGs for any $d>0$ . It is extended to the undirected setting at the end, although only for $d\in\left\{1,2\right\}$ .

#### Vertices.

The vertex set $V$ consists of all $(d+2)$ -dimensional grid points on $[d]\times[4Dr]^{d+1}$ . So we have $|V|=\Theta(dD^{d+1}r^{d+1})$ , as claimed in Item 1.

#### Edges.

For each $i\in[d]$ , $\mathbf{u}\in[4Dr]^{d+1}$ , and $\mathbf{v}=(y,z)\in\mathcal{V}(r)$ , the edge set $E$ contains an edge from $(i,\mathbf{u})$ to $((i\bmod d)+1,\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{v}))$ , if it does not go outside the grid, where $\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{v})$ is the $(d+1)$ -dimensional vector with all zero coordinates except that the $i$ -th and the $(i+1)$ -th coordinates are $y,z$ respectively. So we have $|E|=\Theta(|V|\cdot\Delta)$ , where $\Delta=|\mathcal{V}(r)|=\Theta(r^{2/3})$ by Lemma 2.1, as claimed in Item 1.

#### Critical paths.

*Algorithm 3 The algorithm to construct $\mathcal{P}$ .*

```
1: Let $\mathcal{P}\leftarrow\emptyset$ .
2: for $\mathbf{v}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{v}_{d}\in\mathcal{V}(r)$ do
3: Let $E^{\prime}\leftarrow E$ .
4: repeat
5: Let $P=((i_{1},\mathbf{u}_{1}),\dots,(i_{dD+1},\mathbf{u}_{dD+1}))$ be a path in $E^{\prime}$ such that for all $j\in[dD]$ ,

$$ (i_{j+1},\mathbf{u}_{j+1})=((i_{j}\bmod d)+1,\mathbf{u}_{j}+\mathbf{e}_{i_{j}}(\mathbf{v}_{i_{j}})). $$
6: Let $\mathcal{P}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\cup\left\{P\right\}$ and $E^{\prime}\leftarrow E^{\prime}\setminus P$ .
7: until No $P$ exists.
```

The set of critical paths $\mathcal{P}$ is constructed by Algorithm 3. Item 2a follows directly from the construction.

For Item 2b, observe that each $P\in\mathcal{P}$ uniquely determines its first vertex $(i_{1},\mathbf{u}_{1})$ and $d$ direction vectors $\mathbf{v}_{i}=(y_{i},z_{i})$ for $i\in[d]$ , and vice versa. Also, its last vertex is

$$ (i_{dD+1}=i_{1},\mathbf{u}_{dD+1}=\mathbf{u}_{1}+D\cdot\sum_{i\in[d]}\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{v}_{i})). $$

Let $P^{\prime}$ be any shortest path from $(i_{1},\mathbf{u}_{1})$ to $(i_{dD+1},\mathbf{u}_{dD+1})$ in $G$ . Since $P^{\prime}$ is a shortest path, we can get $|P^{\prime}|\leq|P|=dD$ . In fact, $|P^{\prime}|=dD^{\prime}$ for some $D^{\prime}\leq D$ due to the construction of the edge set $E$ . So $P^{\prime}=((i^{\prime}_{1}=i_{1},\mathbf{u}^{\prime}_{1}=\mathbf{u}_{1}),\dots,(i^{\prime}_{dD^{\prime}+1}=i_{dD+1},\mathbf{u}^{\prime}_{dD^{\prime}+1}=\mathbf{u}_{dD+1}))$ . Furthermore, $P^{\prime}$ induces direction vectors $\mathbf{v}_{i,j}=(y_{i,j},z_{i,j})$ for $i\in[d]$ and $j\in[D^{\prime}]$ such that

$$ \displaystyle D\cdot y_{1} \displaystyle=\sum_{j\in[D^{\prime}]}y_{1,j}, \displaystyle D\cdot z_{i}+D\cdot y_{i+1} \displaystyle=\sum_{j\in[D^{\prime}]}z_{i,j}+\sum_{j\in[D^{\prime}]}y_{i+1,j},\qquad\forall i\in[d-1] \displaystyle D\cdot z_{d} \displaystyle=\sum_{j\in[D^{\prime}]}z_{d,j}. $$

We prove by induction on $d$ that it implies $D^{\prime}=D$ and $\mathbf{v}_{i,j}=\mathbf{v}_{i}$ for all $i\in[d]$ and $j\in[D]$ . The base case is $d=1$ , where we have

$$ D\cdot\mathbf{v}_{1}=\sum_{j\in[D^{\prime}]}\mathbf{v}_{1,j}. $$

The claim then follows from strict convexity of $\mathcal{V}(r)$ as $D^{\prime}\leq D$ . Now consider $d>1$ . Since

$$ D\cdot z_{d}=\sum_{j\in[D^{\prime}]}z_{d,j}, $$

again by strict convexity of $\mathcal{V}(r)$ , we can get

$$ \displaystyle D\cdot y_{d}\geq\sum_{j\in[D^{\prime}]}y_{d,j}. $$

If Eq. 2 is actually an equality, by Eq. 1, we also have

$$ D\cdot z_{d-1}=\sum_{j\in[D^{\prime}]}z_{d-1,j}. $$

Thus, the claim follows from the inductive hypothesis for $d-1$ and the base case. Otherwise, Eq. 2 is a strict inequality, implying that

$$ D\cdot z_{d-1}<\sum_{j\in[D^{\prime}]}z_{d-1,j}, $$

due to Eq. 1. By repeatedly applying the strict convexity argument, we would finally conclude

$$ D\cdot y_{1}>\sum_{j\in[D^{\prime}]}y_{1,j}, $$

a contradiction.

Now we show Item 2c. Fix $P,P^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}$ . By Algorithm 3, $P\cap P^{\prime}=\emptyset$ if they use the same $d$ direction vectors, as they would be added to $\mathcal{P}$ in the same iteration of the for loop. Otherwise, they must use different sets of $d$ direction vectors. Observe that Item 2b also implies $P\cap P^{\prime}$ can only be a consecutive subpath of both $P,P^{\prime}$ . Meanwhile, any path of $d$ edges uniquely determines all $d$ direction vectors. Altogether, it must be that $|P\cap P^{\prime}|<d$ .

To see the size of $\mathcal{P}$ , it is sufficient to show that each iteration of the for loop in Algorithm 3 adds $\Theta(|V|/(dD))$ critical paths. Fix an iteration for $\mathbf{v}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{v}_{d}$ , which uses only the edges from $(i,\mathbf{u})$ to $((i\bmod d)+1,\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{e}_{i}(\mathbf{v}_{i}))$ for $i\in[d]$ and $\mathbf{u}\in[4Dr]^{d+1}$ . Note that each vertex $(i,\mathbf{u})$ with $i\in[d]$ and $\mathbf{u}\in[2Dr]^{d+1}$ has one such edge. Let $E^{\prime\prime}$ be the set of these $|V|/2^{d+1}$ edges and $\mathcal{P}^{\prime}$ the set of critical paths added in this iteration. We claim that $|\mathcal{P}^{\prime}|=\Theta(|E^{\prime\prime}|/(dD))=\Theta(|V|/(dD))$ , as desired.

Regarding the claim, consider an unused edge $e\in E^{\prime\prime}$ from $(i^{\prime},\mathbf{u})$ to $((i^{\prime}\bmod d)+1,\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{e}_{i^{\prime}}(\mathbf{v}_{i^{\prime}}))$ for some $i^{\prime}\in[d]$ and $\mathbf{u}\in[2Dr]^{d+1}$ . Let $P^{\prime}$ be the unique path from $(i^{\prime},\mathbf{u})$ with $dD$ edges, by following the directions $\mathbf{v}_{i}$ alternately. $P^{\prime}$ is well defined as $\mathbf{u}\in[2Dr]^{d+1}$ and each of its coordinates increases by at most $2Dr$ . Since $e$ is unused, there exists $P\in\mathcal{P}^{\prime}$ such that $P\cap P^{\prime}\neq\emptyset$ . Observe that this happens at most $dD$ times for any fixed $P$ , one for each of $dD$ “backtracing” steps in the directions $-\mathbf{v}_{i}$ alternately. So each such unused edge $e\in E^{\prime\prime}$ can be paired with a unique edge of $P$ . In turn, this means $E^{\prime\prime}$ has at most $|\mathcal{P}^{\prime}|\cdot dD$ unused edges and at most $|\mathcal{P}^{\prime}|\cdot dD$ used edges. Combined with $|E^{\prime\prime}|=|V|/2^{d+1}$ , we can get

$$ 2|\mathcal{P}^{\prime}|\cdot dD\geq|V|/2^{d+1}, $$

concluding the proof.

#### From directed to undirected.

In fact, almost identical arguments still work if the directions of the edges are eliminated, except that we now need to show that each critical path $P\in\mathcal{P}$ found by Algorithm 3 remains the unique shortest path between its endpoints. This is necessary because each edge can now be traversed in both directions. We show that such uniqueness indeed holds for $d\in\left\{1,2\right\}$ , which is sufficient for our purposes, in the rest of this section.

The case of $d=1$ follows straightforwardly from strict convexity. To see this, each critical path $P\in\mathcal{P}$ must has the form $s=(1,\mathbf{u}),(1,\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}),\dots,t=(1,\mathbf{u}+D\cdot\mathbf{v})$ , for some $\mathbf{u}\in[4Dr]^{2}$ and $\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{V}(r)$ . Due to strict convexity, this is the unique $s$ - $t$ path with at most $D$ edges, each of which corresponds to a vector in $\mathcal{V}(r)\cup(-\mathcal{V}(r))\subseteq\mathcal{B}(r)$ .

For $d=2$ , fix a critical path $P$ between $s=(i,\mathbf{u})$ and $t=(i,\mathbf{u}^{\prime})$ for some $i\in[2]$ and $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{u}^{\prime}\in[4Dr]^{3}$ . Without loss of generality, assume $i=1$ . The case of $i=2$ is symmetric. Let $\mathbf{v}_{1}=(y_{1},z_{1}),\mathbf{v}_{2}=(y_{2},z_{2})\in\mathcal{V}(r)$ be the two direction vectors induced by $P$ . Let $P^{\prime}$ be any path between $s$ and $t^{\prime}=(1,\mathbf{u}^{\prime\prime})$ for some $\mathbf{u}^{\prime\prime}\in[4Dr]^{3}$ , with at most $2D$ edges. We claim that $P$ is the unique such path maximizing $\langle\mathbf{u}^{\prime\prime}-\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}^{\prime}\rangle$ , where $\mathbf{v}^{\prime}=(y_{1}/z_{1},1,z_{2}/y_{2})$ . Observe that our constructed graph is bipartite for $d=2$ . As a result, each odd step of $P^{\prime}$ either traverses an edge corresponding to $\mathbf{e}_{1}(\mathbf{v}^{\prime}_{1})$ for some $\mathbf{v}^{\prime}_{1}\in\mathcal{V}(r)$ in the forward direction, or traverses an edge corresponding to $\mathbf{e}_{2}(\mathbf{v}^{\prime}_{2})$ for some $\mathbf{v}^{\prime}_{2}\in\mathcal{V}(r)$ in the backward direction. In the former case, $\langle\mathbf{e}_{1}(\mathbf{v}^{\prime}_{1}),\mathbf{v}^{\prime}\rangle>0$ and $\mathbf{v}^{\prime}_{1}=\mathbf{v}_{1}$ is the unique maximizer due to strict convexity. In the latter case, we always have $\langle-\mathbf{e}_{2}(\mathbf{v}^{\prime}_{2}),\mathbf{v}^{\prime}\rangle<0$ because $\mathbf{v}^{\prime}_{2}\in\mathcal{V}(r)$ can only have positive coordinates by definition. Thus, $P^{\prime}$ can maximize $\langle\mathbf{u}^{\prime\prime}-\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}^{\prime}\rangle$ only if it traverses the edge corresponding to $\mathbf{e}_{1}(\mathbf{v}_{1})$ in the forward direction, as does $P$ . A similar analysis holds for even steps. This concludes the proof of the claim. Altogether, $P$ must be the unique $s$ - $t$ shortest path. ∎

#### Proof.

The starting point is a construction of [10], originally introduced in the context of reachability and distance preservers. At a high level, the graph is obtained via obstacle products, where both the inner and the outer graphs use constructions of [16], summarized in Lemma 2.6.

The outer graph has $3$ layers of high dimensional grids. Regarding the inner graph, for reachability and distance preservers as in [10], it suffices to use $2$ -dimensional grids in each layer because the lower bounds are typically concerned with $\mathcal{O}(n)$ -size preservers, as preservers of size $\mathcal{O}(m)$ make little sense. For us, to obtain $m^{1+\Omega(1)}$ lower bounds on certification complexity, we have to first apply alternation products to increase the number of critical paths. This is also by now the standard way of extending diameter lower bounds on $\mathcal{O}(n)$ -size shortcuts to $\mathcal{O}(m)$ -size shortcuts. Specifically, we use the improved alternation product of [21] as given in Lemma 2.7.

Readers are referred to for example [12, 2, 1, 8, 7] for any necessary background knowledge and more detailed discussion on reachability and distance preservers, as well as alternation and obstacle products.

In the rest of this section, we use subscripts $\mathsf{O},\mathsf{I}$ to distinguish between variables for the outer and the inner graphs. Concretely, set $d_{\mathsf{O}}=\sqrt{\log n_{\mathsf{O}}}$ and $D_{\mathsf{O}}=3$ for the outer graph $G_{\mathsf{O}}$ . Moreover, since critical paths in $G_{\mathsf{O}}$ are edge-disjoint, $(x,s^{(v)})$ is the only edge in $G$ from $x$ to any vertex in $G^{(v)}$ . Similarly, $(t^{(v)},y)$ is the only edge in $G$ from any vertex in $G^{(v)}$ to $y$ . As a result, the uniqueness of $s$ - $t$ path in $G_{\mathsf{I}}$ implies the uniqueness of $x$ - $y$ path in $G$ , hence proving Item 3b. To see Item 3c, consider any two critical paths $P,P^{\prime}$ in $G$ obtained from critical paths $(x,v,y),(x^{\prime},v^{\prime},y^{\prime})$ in $G_{\mathsf{O}}$ respectively, which are edge-disjoint by Item 2c of Lemma 2.6. If they are actually vertex-disjoint in $G_{\mathsf{O}}$ , then $P,P^{\prime}$ are also vertex-disjoint in $G$ . If $x=x^{\prime}$ or $y=y^{\prime}$ , we must have $v\neq v^{\prime}$ , so $P,P^{\prime}$ share a single vertex, namely either $x$ or $y$ , in $G$ as well. Otherwise, $v=v^{\prime}$ . In such case, $P,P^{\prime}$ must follow two distinct critical paths in $G^{(v)}$ . Thus, their intersection is at most one edge by Item 2c of Lemma 2.7.

Finally, we calculate the total number of edges and of critical paths in $G$ . By construction, it has $m=\Theta(m_{\mathsf{O}}+n_{\mathsf{O}}m_{\mathsf{I}})=\Theta(n_{\mathsf{O}}n_{\mathsf{I}}\Delta_{\mathsf{I}})=\Theta(n\Delta_{\mathsf{I}})$ . Meanwhile, we have $|\mathcal{P}|=|\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{O}}|=\Theta(n_{\mathsf{O}}\Delta_{\mathsf{O}})=\Theta(n_{\mathsf{O}}|\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{I}}|)=\Theta(n_{\mathsf{O}}n_{\mathsf{I}}\Delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{2}/D_{\mathsf{I}})=\Theta(n\Delta_{\mathsf{I}}^{2}/D)$ . Note that $\Delta_{\mathsf{I}}=\Theta(n_{\mathsf{I}}^{2\varepsilon/3})=n^{8\varepsilon/21-o(\varepsilon)}$ . Therefore, adjusting $\varepsilon$ by an appropriate constant factor in the construction concludes the proof. ∎

## Appendix C Treaps

A treap [3] is a randomized balanced binary tree data structure representing an ordered sequence $S=s_{1},\dots,s_{n}$ of elements, each of which is associated with a randomly sampled priority $p(s_{i})$ . The layout of the treap is entirely determined by the sequence $S$ and the priorities: the root of the treap is the element $s_{j}$ of minimum priority $p(s_{j})$ , its left child is the root of a treap built on elements $s_{1},\dots,s_{j-1}$ , and its right child is the root of a treap built on elements $s_{j+1},\dots,s_{n}$ (using the same global priorities $p(e_{i})$ ). Each vertex also stores the size of its subtree.

*Figure 5: Two treaps on sequences ABCDE and FGHIJ respectively, with the priorities represented by y-coordinates, vertices of smaller priority being higher up.*

Note that the depth of a treap on an $n$ -length sequence is $O(\log n)$ with high probability: the minimum-priority element is in the middle half of elements with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ , in which case the sequences for both the left and right subtrees are a constant fraction smaller. Furthermore, given fixed sampled priorities, a treap has the same layout and in particular depth regardless of the operations that produced it. Thus, for a sequence of $\poly(n)$ operations on a number of treaps of total size $n$ , each treap produced has depth $O(\log n)$ with high probability.

A treap supports two main operations:

- • Join: given two treaps with sequences $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ , construct a treap for the sequence $S=S_{1}S_{2}$ . This operation can be performed in time proportional to the depth of the resulting treap, which is $O(\log|S|)$ with high probability.

- • Split: given a treap and a split point $k$ , split the treap into two treaps for the prefix $S_{1}$ and suffix $S_{2}$ of the sequence $S$ , where $|S_{1}|=k$ and $|S_{2}|=|S|-k$ . This operation can be performed in time proportional to the depth of the input treap, which is $O(\log|S|)$ with high probability.

Both of these operations are simple to implement recursively. Specifically, the join operation on two treaps can be performed as follows:

- 1. Set the root of the result to be the lower-priority root of the two input treaps. Suppose this is the root of the left treap.

- 2. Recursively join the right subtree of the left treap’s root and the right treap, to form the treap for the subsequence right of the root.

- 3. Set the right subtree of the root to be the result of this merge.

The split operation on a treap and a split point $k$ can be performed as follows:

- 1. If the left subtree has size at least $k$ , recursively split it, set the right tree of the recursive split to be the new left subtree, and return the left tree of the recursive split and the old root.

- 2. Otherwise, if the left subtree has size strictly less than $k$ , recursively split the right subtree at $k-\text{size of the left subtree}-1$ . Set the left tree of the recursive split to be the new right subtree, and return the old root and the right tree of the recursive split.

The subtree sizes can be maintained by updating the size whenever a child is changed or recursion returns to a vertex.
